course.title: Python for Data Analysis
course.description: Follow real Python examples from first variables to a checked Pandas report.
course.audience: An adult new to Python; basic arithmetic and familiarity with rows and columns are sufficient.

paragraphs: Data analysis starts with a pile of values: sales figures, survey answers, dates, and names typed by hand. Turning that pile into a figure you can report means deciding which rows count, what a blank cell means and which numbers belong together, and when those decisions are written down as a short Python program they can be run again next month on new data, read by a colleague and corrected when one of them turns out to be wrong, which a series of clicks in a spreadsheet cannot be.

Most of that work in Python is done with two libraries: NumPy, which calculates on whole arrays of numbers at once, and pandas, which holds a table with named columns and labelled rows. Both are quick to write and easy to misread, because the mistakes that cost the most in analysis seldom raise an error. A price stored as text, a blank cell treated as zero or a lookup table that lists one shop twice will each produce a plausible number, so knowing exactly what a line does, well enough to predict its result before it runs, is what lets you notice when a figure is wrong and say why the one you report is right.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a short Python program and say what each name holds at every line.
You'll be able to cut text, lists and arrays down to exactly the values you need.
You'll be able to load a table, clean it and deal with missing values using pandas.
You'll be able to group, merge and reshape tables into a summary you can trust.
You'll be able to check a finished report for mistakes.
introduction.prerequisites: Basic arithmetic and some familiarity with rows and columns are enough, and you do not need to have programmed before.

lessons.title: Follow a value through a program

lead.text: Take the line `price = 4`. Python works out whatever stands to the right of the equals sign, which here is simply the number 4, and stores the result under the name on the left, so that any *later* line can ask for `price` and get 4 back. A line that does this is called an **assignment**.

In `total = price * 3`, Python looks up `price`, multiplies the value it finds by 3, and only then stores the product, so **the name on the left receives a finished value** and not a recipe for calculating it.
Anything after a `#` sign on a line is a **comment**, and Python skips it entirely, so a line such as `# price = 100` changes nothing about what `price` holds.

Return to the three lines from the start of the lesson. When Python reaches `total = price * 3`, `price` holds 4, so the right-hand side comes to 12 and 12 is what is stored under `total`. Nothing in that line tells Python to remember how the 12 was produced.

afterFigure.text: In the first version the last line changes `price` to 6, yet `total` stays at 12, because **the multiplication ran once, when its own line ran**. A spreadsheet behaves differently, since a spreadsheet formula is recalculated whenever the figures it refers to change, but a Python name holds a result and not a rule.

To get 18 the multiplication has to run again after `price` changes, which is what the fourth line of the second version does. Reading a program therefore means following the lines in the order they run and noting what each name holds *at that moment*.

cases.label: Price changes last
cases.code:
price = 4
total = price * 3
price = 6

cases.label: Total recalculated
cases.code:
price = 4
total = price * 3
price = 6
total = price * 3

lead.text: Giving a name a second value is called **reassignment**, and the old value is simply replaced: after `price = 4` and then `price = 6`, the name `price` holds 6 and nothing is left of the 4. Because the right-hand side is worked out before anything is stored, a line may use the very name it is about to replace. In `x = x + 2`, Python looks up the current `x`, adds 2, and stores the result back under `x`, so that an `x` holding 3 holds 5 afterwards.

In algebra the statement x = x + 2 could never be true, which is a useful reminder that the equals sign in Python is an [[assignment|A line such as price = 4 that stores a value under a name. Met in 'Assignment'.]] and not a claim.

The pattern is common enough to have a shorthand: `x += 2` means exactly `x = x + 2`, and `-=`, `*=` and `/=` work the same way for the other operations. A line such as `count += 3` is the usual way to keep a running total, and each time it runs it starts from whatever `count` holds *now*.

cases.label: With a comment
cases.code:
amount = 7
# amount = 100
print(amount)

cases.label: Without the comment
cases.code:
amount = 7
amount = 100
print(amount)

lead.text: Much data analysis is done in a **notebook**, a document that mixes code with its results and is divided into **cells**, each holding a few lines of code that you run one at a time. Running a cell sends its lines to a program called the **kernel**, which carries out the Python and holds every name created so far, so that a name set in one cell can be used by any cell you run afterwards.

The kernel remembers what has been *run* and not what is written on the page, so if you edit a cell and do not run it again, the kernel still holds the values from the last run. Restarting the kernel clears every name.

steps.headline: Running the cell count += 3 twice, with count starting at 2

lead.text: A cell that changes a name starts from whatever the [[kernel|The program that runs a notebook's Python and holds its names. Met in 'Notebooks and kernels'.]] holds. Follow `count` through two runs of the same cell.

workedSteps.text: One cell sets count to 2, and the kernel stores it.
Run the cell `count += 3` once. Python takes the current `count`, 2, adds 3 and stores 5.
Run the same cell again. The result is 8.
Printing count shows 8.

cases.label: Run once
cases.code:
count = 2
count += 3
print(count)

cases.label: Run twice
cases.code:
count = 2
count += 3
count += 3
print(count)

steps.headline: Three runs of count += 4, starting from 1

lead.text: Now the same cell with a different step.

workedSteps.text: Start with `count = 1`. The first run of `count += 4` stores 5.
The second run starts from the 5 that the kernel holds.
The third run starts from the value that the second run left.

lead.text: Suppose cell 1 sets `width = 3`, cell 2 sets `area = width * 2`, and cell 3 sets `width = 8`. Run in that order, the cells leave `area` at 6. If you then run cell 2 again, it reads the newer `width` and `area` becomes 16, even though not a single line was edited.

A notebook is therefore reproducible only if it gives the same results when the kernel is restarted and every cell is run once, from the top, in order. Before you share a notebook, **restart the kernel and run all the cells**: any cell that fails, or that changes a result, was relying on a run the page does not show.

lessons.orientation: Follow what each name holds as a program runs, line by line and cell by cell.
lessons.reviewLabel: Follow a value through a program
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Here are three lines of Python: `price = 4`, then `total = price * 3`, then `price = 6`. Read as arithmetic, the first two lines make `total` 12, and the third then changes `price`, which raises the question of whether `total` is still 12 or has become 18 to match the new price.
The answer depends on what Python does when it meets each line, and on the order in which the lines run, so you need to be able to say, at any line, which value each name is holding.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what every name holds at each line of a short program and across the cells of a notebook.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later lesson reaches its data through names, so a wrong picture of what a name holds spoils whatever follows.

recap.keyIdea: An assignment stores a finished value under a name, and the name keeps that value until a line that runs gives it another.

blocks.text: A line such as `total = price * 3` works out its right-hand side **once** and stores the result, so `total` does not follow `price` when `price` changes later, and a line such as `count += 3` starts from whatever `count` holds now. In a notebook the [[kernel|The program that runs a notebook's Python and holds its names. Met in 'Notebooks and kernels'.]] keeps every name between cells, so what a name holds depends on which cells have *run* and in what order, and restarting and running everything from the top is the check that the notebook says what it does.

recap.nextHook: Every name so far held a whole number, but data also arrives as decimals and as text that only looks like a number, and Python treats these differently. The next lesson separates them.

lessons.title: Know what a number means

lead.text: Every value in Python has a **type**, which says what kind of thing the value is and therefore what can be done with it. A whole number such as 12 has the type **int**, while anything written between quotation marks, such as `'12'`, has the type **str**, short for string, which is a sequence of characters.

afterFigure.text: Conversion is the usual repair when numbers have arrived as text, and `int()` is **the explicit step that turns characters into a number**. It works only when the text really does spell a whole number, so `int('12')` gives 12 while `int('twelve')` stops with an error.

cases.label: Plus on strings
cases.code:
a = '12'
b = '3'
result = a + b

cases.label: Plus after int()
cases.code:
a = '12'
b = '3'
result = int(a) + int(b)

lead.text: Dividing 17 by 5 can be asked in three ways. The slash gives the exact answer, `17 / 5` = 3.4, a number with a decimal point, which has the type **float**. **Floor division**, written `//`, gives only the whole number of times 5 fits into 17, which is 3 and is called the quotient, and the percent sign gives the **remainder**, the 2 that is left over, so that `17 % 5` is 2.
The three results are linked, because the quotient times the divisor, plus the remainder, gives back the number you started with: 3 * 5 + 2 is 17.
Powers have an operator of their own, so Python writes `2 ** 3` for two to the power of three, which is 8.

Dividing 11 by 4 gives 2.75, so the quotient is 2 and the remainder is 3, as the first case of the figure shows. Negative numbers need one more rule, because the whole number of times a divisor fits is ambiguous once the exact answer lies below zero. Floor division always rounds *down*, to the next whole number towards minus infinity, and not towards zero.

afterFigure.text: For −11 divided by 4 the exact answer is −2.75. The whole numbers on either side are −3 and −2, and rounding down picks −3, so `−11 // 4` is −3 and not −2. The remainder then keeps the relationship intact, since −3 * 4 + 1 is −11, which is why `−11 % 4` is 1. In Python **the remainder takes the sign of the divisor**, so with a positive divisor it is never negative.

cases.label: Positive 11 by 4
cases.code:
a = 11
b = 4
quotient = a // b
remainder = a % b
exact = a / b

cases.label: Negative −11 by 4
cases.code:
a = -11
b = 4
quotient = a // b
remainder = a % b
exact = a / b

lead.text: Floor division of a negative number follows the same steps every time: find the exact answer, find the whole numbers on either side of it, and take the smaller one.

workedSteps.text: Work out the exact answer first.
The whole numbers on either side of −3.5 are −4 and −3.
Floor division takes the smaller one.
The remainder is what is left over: −7 − (−4 * 2) = 1.

lead.text: Now the same steps for a new pair of numbers.

workedSteps.text: The exact answer is −13 / 5.
Floor division rounds the exact answer down to a whole number.
The remainder is what is left of −13 once the whole groups of 5 found above have been taken away.

lead.text: A [[float|A number with a decimal point, such as 3.4. Met in 'Three kinds of division'.]] is stored in binary, and most decimal fractions cannot be written exactly in binary, in the same way that one third cannot be written exactly with a finite number of decimal digits. Python therefore stores the nearest value it can, and a sum of floats can come out a very small distance from the decimal answer you expect. The error is far too small to matter in a total, but it is large enough to matter when two floats are compared with `==`, because `==` asks whether the stored values are *identical* and not whether they are close.

Whole numbers have no such problem. An `int` is exact whatever its size, since Python widens it as needed, and so counts of rows or of people should stay as ints. The practical rule for floats is to **compare them after rounding, or within a tolerance**, and never to trust `==` on the result of decimal arithmetic.

cases.label: A very large int
cases.code:
value = 2 ** 40
exact = value + 1

cases.label: A sum of decimals
cases.code:
total = 0.1 + 0.2
equal = total == 0.3

lead.text: A comparison such as `3 < 5` produces a value of the type **bool**, which has only two values, `True` and `False`. Python also treats other values as true or false whenever it needs to, for example when `bool()` is applied to them or in a condition. Zero of any numeric type and the empty string count as `False`, and everything else counts as `True`, so `bool(3)` is `True`, `bool(0.0)` is `False`, `bool('hello')` is `True` and `bool('')` is `False`.

A string is false only when it is empty, so a non-empty string such as `'no'` is `True` however negative it sounds. This matters in data work because a cell read from a file arrives as [[text|A value written between quotation marks, of the type str. Met in 'Text and numbers'.]], and a column of `'FALSE'` strings will test as `True` until it has been converted.

cases.label: The bool False
cases.code:
value = False
flag = bool(value)

cases.label: The text 'False'
cases.code:
value = 'False'
flag = bool(value)

lessons.orientation: Tell text from numbers, choose between the three divisions and know when a comparison can be trusted.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Python will say that 12 + 3 is 15, and it will also say that '12' + '3' is '123', and both answers are right. The difference is a pair of quotation marks: with them, 12 is no longer a number but two characters, a 1 followed by a 2, and the plus sign joins characters end to end instead of adding quantities.

Data arrives with exactly this ambiguity, because a column of prices read from a file may hold the characters of numbers and not the numbers themselves, and a sum taken over it will be wrong without any error to warn you.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell text from numbers, choose the right kind of division, and know when a comparison can be trusted.
intro.whyItMatters: Prices that arrive as text, rounded totals and every-third-row questions all depend on these distinctions.

recap.keyIdea: A value's type decides what an operation does, so check that a number is really a number before doing arithmetic on it.

blocks.text: Quotation marks make **text**, and plus joins text instead of adding it until `int()` converts it to a number. Python divides in three ways: `/` gives the exact float, `//` gives the quotient by rounding *down*, and `%` gives the remainder, which takes the sign of the divisor. Floats are approximate and so should not be compared with `==`, and a value tests as `False` only when it is zero or empty, which makes the text `'False'` `True`.

recap.nextHook: Text has now appeared in two lessons without being looked at closely. The next lesson cuts it up by position and applies methods to it.

lessons.title: Take exactly the text you need

lead.text: A string is a row of characters, and Python gives each one a number that records where it stands. The count starts at *zero*, so in `'PLANET'` the P is at position 0, the L at 1, the A at 2, the N at 3, the E at 4 and the T at 5. This number is called the **index**, and `label[2]` means the character at index 2 of `label`, which is `'A'` when `label` holds `'PLANET'`.

The built-in function `len()` gives the number of characters, which for `'PLANET'` is 6. Because **the first index is 0**, the last index is always one less than the length, here 5, and an index of 6 would lie past the end. Python also numbers from the back, so that −1 is the last character, −2 the one before it, and so on.

To take several characters at once, write two indexes inside the brackets with a colon between them. The result is called a **slice**, and `label[1:4]` starts at index 1 and *stops* at index 4, so it holds the characters at indexes 1, 2 and 3. **The stop is not included**, which means a slice has stop − start characters: here 4 − 1 = 3.

afterFigure.text: The second case counts from the back: `label[-2:]` starts at −2, which is the E, and has no stop, so it carries on to the end of the word and returns `'ET'`.

cases.label: From the front
cases.code:
label = 'PLANET'
part = label[1:4]

cases.label: From the back
cases.code:
label = 'PLANET'
part = label[-2:]

lead.text: An omitted start is taken as **the beginning** of the string and an omitted stop as **its end**, so `label[:3]` holds the first three characters of `'PLANET'`, which are `'PLA'`, and `label[3:]` holds everything from index 3 onwards, which is `'NET'`. The two slices share no character and together rebuild the whole word, so cutting at the same number twice never loses or doubles a letter, and that is the practical reason the stop is excluded.

Negative numbers work in [[slices|A piece taken between a start and a stop; the stop is not included. Met in 'Slicing'.]] as they do for single characters. The slice `label[-3:]` begins three characters from the end and runs to the end, so it holds *the last three characters* however long the string is, and `label[:-1]` holds everything except the last.
To read a slice with a negative start, number the characters from the end of the string first.

workedSteps.text: Number the characters from the back: R is −1, E is −2, T is −3 and N is −4.
The slice starts at −4, which is the N.
Nothing follows the colon.
The slice is 'NTER', which has four characters.

lead.text: Now a slice with both bounds, and as before the stop is not included.

workedSteps.text: The characters are B at 0, A at 1, N at 2, T at 3, E at 4 and R at 5.
workedSteps.math: B0 A1 N2 T3 E4 R5

workedSteps.text: The slice starts at index 1 and stops before index 5.
The slice holds A, N, T and E, so it is `'ANTE'`.
A slice that leaves the stop out, such as `'BANTER'[2:]`, runs from its start to the end of the string.

lead.text: A **method** is a function attached to a value and called with a dot, as in `name.strip()`. The method `strip` removes spaces, tabs and line breaks from both ends of a string, and `upper` changes every letter to a capital, so `'  bay  '.strip().upper()` gives `'BAY'`. Calls can be chained in this way because each one returns a new string for the next to work on.

afterFigure.text: In the figure's second case the same calls are made but their result is not assigned to anything, so `name` still holds `'  bay  '` with its spaces. A string can never be changed once it exists, which is described by saying that strings are **immutable**: a method does not alter the string it is called on but builds a *new* one, and **unless you store the new string under a name it is lost**. The usual remedy is to assign the result back, as in `name = name.strip()`.

cases.label: Result stored
cases.code:
name = '  bay  '
clean = name.strip().upper()

cases.label: Result ignored
cases.code:
name = '  bay  '
name.strip().upper()

lead.text: A tab is invisible, and a newline, the character that ends a line, would break the string across two lines, so Python lets a backslash stand in for them: `'\t'` is a tab and `'\n'` is a newline. Such a pair is called an **escape**, and although it is written with two symbols it is stored as *one* character, so `len('1\t2')` is 3 and not 4.

The same characters turn up whenever text is read from a file, since every line of a text file ends with a newline, which is one reason `strip()` is so often the first method applied to text from outside.

Asking for a single character that does not exist stops the program with an **IndexError**: `'AB'[5]` fails because the string has only the [[indexes|The numbers giving the positions of characters, counted from 0. Met in 'Indexing'.]] 0 and 1. A slice behaves differently, since it *never* fails and returns whatever characters lie within its bounds, which may be fewer than the bounds suggest, or none at all.
A slice whose start lies beyond the end, or whose start is not below its stop, contains nothing, and its value is the **empty string**, written `''` and with a length of 0.

cases.label: A longer string
cases.code:
code = 'ABCDEF'
tail = code[3:20]

cases.label: A shorter string
cases.code:
code = 'AB'
tail = code[3:20]

lessons.orientation: Pick out exactly the characters you want from a string, and clean text without changing the original.
lessons.reviewLabel: Take exactly the text you need
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: The word PLANET has six characters, and the letters LAN sit in the middle of it, in the second, third and fourth places. To pull out exactly those three, Python numbers every position in a string and lets you name a piece by where it starts and where it stops.

Cutting text to size is routine in data work, and a cut that is off by one character keeps the wrong text without raising any error, so the rules, which are few and exact, are worth learning until they are automatic.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to cut a string with a slice, count what the slice contains, and clean text with methods safely.
intro.whyItMatters: A slice that is one character out returns the wrong text without any warning, so the boundaries must be exact.

recap.keyIdea: A slice takes the characters from the start up to but not including the stop, and a string method returns new text that must be stored.

blocks.text: Characters are numbered from **0**, or from −1 at the back, and a slice runs from its start up to *but not including* its stop, with a missing start meaning the beginning and a missing stop meaning the end. A single index past the end raises an `IndexError` while a slice past the end quietly shrinks, and because strings are immutable a method such as `strip()` returns new text that is lost unless it is stored under a name.

recap.nextHook: Strings are one kind of sequence. The next lesson turns to lists, which hold many values and, unlike strings, can be changed in place.

lessons.title: Change a collection without surprises

lead.text: A **list** is written with square brackets and commas, as in `scores = [12, 15, 11]`, and its items are numbered from 0 exactly as the characters of a string are, so `scores[0]` is 12 and `len(scores)` is 3. Unlike a string, a list can be changed after it has been made, which is described by saying that it is **mutable**: the line `scores[0] = 10` replaces the first item, and the method **append** adds one more item at the end, so that `scores.append(14)` leaves the list holding `[10, 15, 11, 14]`.

In both cases the same list has been altered *in place* and no new list has been built. That is a real difference from the string methods of the last lesson, which returned new text and left the original untouched.

Assigning a list to a second name does *not* copy the list. After `b = a`, the names `a` and `b` are two **aliases** for a single list, and a change made through one of them is a change to the list that both see.

afterFigure.text: In the first case `b = a` makes an alias, so appending through `b` grows the list that `a` also points to, and both names show `[2, 5, 8]`. In the second case `b = a.copy()` builds a new list holding the same items, so the append reaches only `b` and `a` is left as `[2, 5]`. **Copying, and not assignment, is what separates two lists**, and code that changes a list it was given should ask whether another name still depends on it.

cases.label: Alias: b = a
cases.code:
a = [2, 5]
b = a
b.append(8)

cases.label: Copy: b = a.copy()
cases.code:
a = [2, 5]
b = a.copy()
b.append(8)

lead.text: The answer is **None**, the value Python uses for *nothing here*. A method that changes a list in place, such as `append`, has finished its work by the time it ends and has nothing further to return, which is the opposite of a string method: a string method must return its result, because the string itself can never change.

This leads to a common mistake. In `items = items.append(9)`, the method first changes the list and then returns `None`, and the assignment stores that `None` under `items`, so the name no longer points to the list. The correct line is simply `items.append(9)`, with nothing assigned.
Follow one list through two ways of writing the same call, and watch what the name items holds at the end of each.

workedSteps.text: The list starts with two items.
Calling append and storing the result under a second name shows what the call returns: items grows and result holds None.
Assigning the call back to items instead stores None under the name that held the list.
The list `[4, 7, 9]` was built, but no name points to it any longer.

cases.label: Result stored apart
cases.code:
items = [4, 7]
result = items.append(9)

cases.label: Result assigned back
cases.code:
items = [4, 7]
items = items.append(9)

lead.text: A list can hold other lists, as in `a = [[1, 2], [3]]`, which has two items, of which the first is itself a list of two. The `copy()` method builds a new outer list, but it fills that list with the *same* inner lists, so the result is called a **shallow copy**: the outer lists are separate and the inner ones are shared.

The consequence follows from what you already know. Appending to the outer copy affects only the copy, but appending to an inner list through the copy, as in `b[0].append(9)`, changes the list that `a` also holds, because both outer lists point to it. A fully independent copy of nested lists needs the function `deepcopy` from Python's `copy` module but the habit of asking **which level is shared** is worth keeping.

steps.headline: Appending to an inner list of a shallow copy

lead.text: Take `a = [[1, 2], [3]]` and make `b = a.copy()`.

workedSteps.text: The copy has a new outer list, but its two items are the same two inner lists that `a` holds.
Then the line `b[0].append(9)` runs.
After that line, `a[0]` is the first inner list that `a` holds.

lead.text: A **tuple** is written with round brackets, as in `pair = ('x', [5])`, and it is indexed and sliced like a list, but it cannot be changed: `pair[0] = 'y'` stops with a `TypeError`, and a tuple has no `append`.

A tuple fixes *which objects* it holds and not what those objects are. If one of its items is a list, the tuple keeps pointing to that same list, and the list can still be changed: `pair[1].append(6)` works, and afterwards the list inside the tuple holds `[5, 6]`.

cases.label: Shallow copy
cases.code:
a = [[1], [2]]
b = a.copy()
b[0].append(3)

cases.label: List in a tuple
cases.code:
record = ('Bay', [1, 2])
record[1].append(3)

lead.text: [[Slices|A piece taken between a start and a stop; the stop is not included. Met in 'Slicing'.]] work on lists as they do on strings: `values[1:3]` runs from index 1 up to but not including index 3, so it holds two items, and it builds a *new* list without changing the old one. The plus sign joins two lists into a longer one, and multiplying a list by a whole number repeats it that many times, so `[0] * 3` builds `[0, 0, 0]`.

afterFigure.text: **Slices, joins and repeats all build new lists**; only the methods that work in place, such as `append`, and assignment to an index alter the original. A slice with no bounds, `values[:]`, is therefore a quick way to make a shallow copy.

cases.label: A slice
cases.code:
values = [3, 6, 9, 12]
result = values[1:3]

cases.label: A repeat
cases.code:
values = [3, 6]
result = values * 2

lessons.orientation: Change lists in place, see which names share a list, and know what a copy or a tuple protects.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Write `scores = [12, 15, 11]` and Python holds three values in order. Unlike a string, which cannot be altered once it exists, a list can have any of its values replaced and new ones added without a new list being made.

The same ability causes the commonest surprise with lists, because a name does not hold a list but points to one, so that when two names point to the same list a change made through either is seen through both. Knowing exactly what is shared and what is separate makes list code predictable.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which names see a change to a list, what a list method returns, and what a copy or a tuple does and does not protect.
intro.whyItMatters: Many bugs in data code come from a list changed through one name while another name still relies on it.

recap.keyIdea: A list is changed in place, so two names for one list see each other's changes, and only a copy gives you a separate list.

blocks.text: A list is *mutable*, and `b = a` gives it a second name, so that only `copy()` produces a separate outer list, and even that **shallow copy** still shares any lists inside. Methods that change a list, such as `append`, return `None`, so their result should not be assigned back, while slices, joins and repeats build new lists. A tuple cannot swap its items, but a list inside it can still change.

recap.nextHook: A list finds an item by its position, which is awkward when you would rather ask for it by name. The next lesson looks things up by key and keeps only distinct values.

lessons.title: Choose the right collection

lead.text: A **dictionary** pairs each label with a value and is written with braces: `stock = {'pen': 3, 'book': 2}`. The label is called a **key** and what it leads to is the value, so `'pen'` is a key and 3 is its value, and `stock['pen']` looks the value up directly, with no counting of positions.

afterFigure.text: Assigning to an existing key *replaces* its value, so `stock['pen'] = 7` leaves two entries with the pen count changed, whereas assigning to a key that is not there *adds* an entry, so `stock['lamp'] = 7` leaves three. The same line **either replaces or adds**, depending on whether the key exists, and the number of keys afterwards tells you which happened.

cases.label: An existing key
cases.code:
stock = {'pen': 3, 'book': 2}
stock['pen'] = 7

cases.label: A new key
cases.code:
stock = {'pen': 3, 'book': 2}
stock['lamp'] = 7

lead.text: Looking up a key that is not there stops the program with a **KeyError**, so a lookup such as `scores['Cy']` fails when no entry for Cy has been made. The test `'Cy' in scores` asks the question first and gives `True` or `False`. Notice that **in checks the keys** and *never* the values, because the keys are the labels that a dictionary is organised around.

The method `get` combines the test and the lookup. It takes a key and a **fallback**, and it returns the stored value when the key exists and the fallback when it does not, so `scores.get('Cy', 0)` gives 0 for a dictionary that has no Cy entry.

steps.headline: Does 3 count as being in stock?

lead.text: Both tests below look inside `stock = {'pen': 3, 'book': 2}`, but they look at different things.

workedSteps.text: The keys are the labels pen and book, and the values are the numbers 3 and 2.
The test 'pen' in stock asks about the keys, and pen is one of them.
The test 3 in stock asks about the keys too, and 3 is a value and not a key.
To ask about the values, look at them explicitly with `stock.values()`.

cases.label: Key and fallback
Value and key

lead.text: A **set** is a collection of distinct values with *no* order and *no* positions. It is written with braces and no colons, as in `{'Bay', 'Hill'}`, and `set()` applied to a list keeps one copy of each value, so a list of visits that mentions Bay twice becomes a set that holds Bay once. Each value in a set is called a **member**, and a set is used mainly to ask whether a value is a member and how many different values there are.

afterFigure.text: The second case adds a new member with the method `add`, which changes the set in place just as `append` changes a list. Adding a value that is already a member changes nothing, because **a set holds each member at most once**. Since a set has no positions, an index such as `shops[0]` is an error, and a **frozenset** is the version that cannot be changed once it is made.

cases.label: From a list
cases.code:
visits = ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay']
shops = set(visits)

cases.label: Adding a member
cases.code:
shops = {'Bay', 'Hill'}
shops.add('Lake')

lead.text: Two sets can be combined by asking which members they share and which they hold between them. The **intersection**, written `a & b`, contains the members found in *both* sets, and the **union**, written `a | b`, contains the members found in *either*, with shared members counted once. The figure applies both to `a = {1, 2, 4}` and `b = {2, 3, 4}`.

afterFigure.text: A third operator, `a - b`, keeps the members of `a` that are not in `b`, which here leaves only 1. Intersection is **the 'and' of membership** and union is **the 'or'**, so a question phrased with both and either maps directly onto these operators.

lead.text: Each collection answers a different question quickly. A list keeps items in order and allows repeats, so it fits values whose position matters. A dictionary answers *what goes with this label*, and a set answers *is this value present, and how many different values are there*.

Dictionary keys and set members must be values that cannot change, such as strings, numbers or tuples of them, which is why a list is refused as a key. A short test settles most decisions: if you will look things up by name, **use a dictionary**; if repeats are only noise, use a set; and if order or repeats matter, use a list. The right choice often removes a loop altogether, since testing membership in a set is typically a single step however many members it holds, whereas a list has to be searched from the front.

lessons.orientation: Look values up by key, keep distinct members in a set, and choose the collection that fits the question.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: The list `[3, 2]` holds two stock counts, but nothing in it says which is which: that the 3 counts pens and the 2 counts books is a fact kept in the programmer's head, and it breaks as soon as an item is added in the middle. A dictionary stores the label with the number, as in `{'pen': 3, 'book': 2}`, so that the count of pens is found by asking for pen and not by remembering a position.

A second kind of question is about membership and not about order. A list of shop visits such as `['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay']` records every visit, but the question *which shops were visited* wants each shop once, and that is what a set stores.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to update and read a dictionary safely, count the distinct members of a set, and choose the collection a question calls for.
intro.whyItMatters: Real tables are full of labels and repeats, and the right collection answers a question about them in one step.

recap.keyIdea: Use a dictionary to go from a key to a value, a set to hold each value once, and choose by the question you will ask.

blocks.text: A dictionary leads from a **key** to a value, so assigning to an existing key replaces its value and assigning to a new key adds one, while `in` tests the keys and `get` supplies a fallback for a missing key. A set holds each member *once*, and its intersection and union answer questions about what two groups share and hold between them.

recap.nextHook: So far every program has run its lines once, from top to bottom. The next lesson makes a program choose between lines and repeat them.

lessons.title: Control which work happens

lead.text: The line `if units >= 10:` asks a question whose answer is `True` or `False`, and the indented lines beneath it run only when the answer is `True`. The question is called a **condition**, and the choice between lines of code that it makes is called a **branch**. The comparison signs are `==` for equal, `!=` for not equal, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`, and the double sign matters, because a single `=` stores a value while `==` asks whether two values are equal.

A chain of `if`, `elif` (short for *else if*) and `else` lists the conditions in order, and Python runs **the first branch whose condition is True** and skips the rest. The `else` branch has no condition and catches whatever remains.

afterFigure.text: In the figure's second case 12 units satisfy the first test at once, and the later tests are never examined, so the fee is 0. The order of the tests therefore matters: if the test for 5 units came first, 12 units would be charged 2.

cases.label: Three units
Twelve units

lead.text: A **for loop** takes each item of a collection in turn and runs its indented lines once for *each*. In `for item in items: total += item`, the name `item` holds the first value on the first pass and the second on the next, and the lines beneath the `for` line are the loop body. The function **range** produces the numbers to loop over: `range(4)` gives 0, 1, 2, 3, and `range(1, 8, 2)` gives 1, 3, 5, 7, which is a start, a stop that is excluded and a step, just as in a [[slice|A piece of a string or list taken between a start and a stop; the stop is not included. Met in 'Slicing'.]].

afterFigure.text: Both cases keep a running total that starts at 0 and has each item added in turn, and a name used in this way is called an **accumulator**. The built-in function `sum()` adds a whole collection in one call, so `sum(range(4))` is also 6, but the loop form is the one that extends to any calculation that must be done for each item.

cases.label: Items 0 to 3
cases.code:
items = list(range(4))
total = 0
for item in items:
    total += item

cases.label: Items 1, 3, 5, 7
cases.code:
items = list(range(1, 8, 2))
total = 0
for item in items:
    total += item

steps.headline: Adding up range(1, 5) one pass at a time

lead.text: Follow the accumulator through each pass of a loop that adds the numbers produced by `range(1, 5)`.

workedSteps.text: The accumulator is set before the loop starts.
The range produces 1, 2, 3 and 4, because the stop is excluded.
On each pass the item is added to the total: 0 + 1, then 1 + 2, then 3 + 3, then 6 + 4.
After the fourth pass the range is used up and the loop ends with the last total.

lead.text: The same loop with a step of 2.

workedSteps.text: The numbers run from 4 in steps of 2 and stop before 10.
The loop body runs once for each value that the range produces.
Each pass adds its item to the accumulator, which starts at 0.

lead.text: A **while loop** repeats its body for as long as its condition is `True`, testing the condition before each pass. A [[for loop|Repeats its body once for each item of a collection. Met in 'For loops'.]] knows how many passes it will make, but a while loop is used when you do *not*, and its body must therefore change something that the condition depends on, because otherwise the test never fails and the loop never ends.

afterFigure.text: In the first case `count` starts at 1 and gains 2 on each pass, giving 3, 5 and then 7. The test `count < 6` is made before every pass, so the third pass runs, the value 7 fails the test, and `turns` ends at 3. **The loop stops at the first value that fails the test**, and the body has already run on the last value that passed it, so the final count overshoots the limit.

cases.label: Steps of 2
cases.code:
count = 1
turns = 0
while count < 6:
    count += 2
    turns += 1

cases.label: Steps of 3
cases.code:
count = 1
turns = 0
while count < 6:
    count += 3
    turns += 1

lead.text: The word `and` gives `True` only when both parts are `True`, `or` gives `True` when at least one part is, and `not` reverses a single answer. So `x > 3 and x < 9` asks whether `x` lies between 3 and 9, while `x < 2 or x > 8` asks whether it lies outside that stretch.

The sign `&` between two integers works on their **binary** digits, the 0s and 1s in which a computer stores them, and it keeps a digit only where both numbers have a 1. Written in binary, 12 is 1100 and 10 is 1010, so `12 & 10` keeps only the leading 1 and is 1000, which is 8, and `12 | 10` keeps a digit where either has a 1 and is 1110, which is 14. In an if statement you write `and`, `or` and `not`; later lessons use `&` and `|` to combine conditions on whole columns of a table.

Tests and loops combine naturally. Suppose a list holds 4, 9, 12 and 7, and you want to know how many of its items are above 5 and below 10. A counter starts at 0, a for loop visits each item in turn, an if inside the loop body decides whether the item passes, and *only then* is the counter increased: `count += 1`.

Traced by hand, the 4 fails the test and the count stays at 0, the 9 passes and the count becomes 1, the 12 fails, and the 7 passes and brings the count to 2. The loop decides **what is visited** and the test decides **what is counted**, and keeping those two jobs separate makes a program easy to read back.

cases.label: and between conditions
cases.code:
x = 6
within = x > 3 and x < 9

cases.label: & between integers
cases.code:
a = 6
b = 3
both_bits = a & b

lessons.orientation: Trace which lines of a program run, and how many times, through tests and repetition.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Take a fee that depends on the number of units bought: 4 for fewer than five units, 2 from five units and 0 from ten. A line such as `fee = 4` cannot express that rule, because a program that runs each of its lines once, in order, does the same thing whatever the number of units. Python makes it possible with a test, which lets the program choose which lines to run, and with a loop, which runs the same lines again with a new value each time.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace which branch runs, how many times a loop repeats, and whether a combined condition is True.
intro.whyItMatters: Totals, filters and repeated clean-ups all rest on choosing lines to run and counting passes correctly.

recap.keyIdea: A branch runs only when its condition holds, and a loop repeats its body until its range runs out or its test fails.

blocks.text: An if chain runs the **first** branch whose condition is `True`, a for loop runs its body once for each item that `range` produces, and a while loop tests its condition before every pass and stops at the first value that fails. Conditions combine with `and`, `or` and `not`, and an accumulator inside a loop, guarded by a test, counts or totals exactly the items you intend.

recap.nextHook: Tests and loops are easier to reuse once they are given a name. The next lesson wraps a calculation in a function and borrows ready-made ones with import.

lessons.title: Turn a calculation into a tool

lead.text: A **function** is a calculation with a name, defined once and used wherever it is needed. The definition `def area(width, height): return width * height` introduces the name `area` and two **parameters**, `width` and `height`, which stand for values the function has not yet been given. A call such as `area(3, 5)` supplies those values, called **arguments**, in the same order as the parameters, and Python runs the body with `width` as 3 and `height` as 5.

The word **return** ends the function and sends a value back to the place where it was called, so the call `area(3, 5)` is replaced by 15 and can be used like any other value. Names created inside a function exist *only* while it runs, so a `width` inside one function cannot collide with a `width` elsewhere in the program.

The question you have just answered turns on a distinction that causes real confusion. The function **print** displays a value on the screen for a person to read, whereas `return` hands a value back to the program so that *other lines* can use it. A function that only prints has still finished, and a call to a function with no `return` statement gives back [[None|The value Python uses for nothing here. Met in 'Methods that return None'.]].

afterFigure.text: In the first case `double` returns `x * 2`, so `result` holds 8 and could be added to something else. In the second case the function prints 8 and returns nothing, so the screen shows 8 but `result` holds `None`, and any arithmetic with `result` would fail. A function meant to feed a later calculation **must return its answer**; printing is for showing results to a reader.

cases.label: Return
Print only

lead.text: A parameter can be given a **default**, written in the definition as `rate=5`, which is used whenever a call leaves that argument out. In `def cost(units, rate=5)`, the call `cost(3)` uses the default and works out 3 * 5, while `cost(3, 7)` replaces it. Arguments can also be passed by name, as in `cost(rate=7, units=3)`, which is called a **keyword argument**: each value is matched to the parameter whose name it carries and *not* to a position.

afterFigure.text: **Positional arguments come first and named ones after them**, so `cost(3, rate=7)` is allowed but `cost(rate=7, 3)` is a syntax error.

cases.label: Default used
Both named

steps.headline: Calling cost with a default and with names

lead.text: Follow three calls of one function, whose rate defaults to 4.

workedSteps.text: The definition gives rate a default.
workedSteps.math: def cost(units, rate=4): return units * rate

workedSteps.text: With one argument the default is used, so 3 units cost 3 * 4.
With both arguments named, each value goes to the parameter whose name it carries.
The same names written in the opposite order fill the same parameters and give the same result.

lead.text: The same function, `def cost(units, rate=4): return units * rate`.

workedSteps.text: A positional argument fills the first parameter, and a named one fills the parameter it names, so the first value below is units.
The body of `cost` multiplies `units` by `rate`.
In `cost(rate=6, units=5)` both arguments are named, so the order in which they are written does not decide which parameter each one fills.

lead.text: When a function is called, each parameter becomes a new name for the argument it receives, so a list that is passed in is the *very same* list the caller holds and not a copy. This is the [[alias|Another name for the same list. Met in 'Two names, one list'.]] problem from the lists lesson again: a method such as `append`, called on the parameter, changes the one list that both names reach, and the caller sees the change.

afterFigure.text: In the first case `add_item` appends 9 to the list it was given, so `values` becomes `[1, 2, 9]` although the function returned nothing. In the second case the line `items = [9]` only points the parameter at a new list, which does not touch `values`, so `values` stays `[1, 2]`. Changing the object a name points to **affects everyone who shares it**, while reassigning the name affects **only that name**. A function that should leave its input alone has to copy it first, or build and return a new list.

cases.label: Appending
cases.code:
def add_item(items):
    items.append(9)
values = [1, 2]
add_item(values)

cases.label: Reassigning
cases.code:
def add_item(items):
    items = [9]
values = [1, 2]
add_item(values)

lead.text: A **module** is a collection of ready-made functions and values, and the statement **import** makes one available. After `import math`, the call `math.sqrt(81)` gives 9.0, which is *always* a float, while `math.floor(7.9)` gives 7 and `math.ceil(7.1)` gives 8, since `floor` rounds down and `ceil` rounds up.

The statement `import math as m` gives the module a shorter name, an [[alias|Another name for the same thing. Met in 'Two names, one list'.]], so that the same call is written `m.sqrt(81)`. The data libraries are always imported in this way under conventional short names, `import numpy as np` and `import pandas as pd`, and the lessons that follow begin from those two lines.

cases.label: Full name
cases.code:
import math
result = math.sqrt(81)

cases.label: Short name
cases.code:
import math as m
result = m.sqrt(81)

lessons.orientation: Define a function, pass it values, tell returning from printing, and import ready-made ones.
lessons.reviewLabel: Turn a calculation into a tool
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: The calculation `units * rate` might be needed in a dozen places in one program. Writing it out each time invites a slip in one of them, and changing the rate means finding all twelve, whereas a function gives the calculation a name, so that each place that needs it calls the name and the calculation itself lives in exactly one spot.

Python also ships with hundreds of ready-made functions, so nearly every line of analysis you write will call a function, pass it values and use what it gives back. Reading such a line correctly means knowing what comes back from a call, which is not always what appears on the screen, and what a function is able to change in the values you hand it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a function's definition and calls, tell a printed value from a returned one, and import and use a module.
intro.whyItMatters: Every library call in the rest of the course is a function call, and its result is what it returns.

recap.keyIdea: A function returns a value to its caller, and printing a value is not the same as returning it.

blocks.text: A function is defined once with parameters, called with arguments, and **returns** a value that replaces the call, while a function that only prints gives back `None`. Defaults fill in a missing argument and keyword arguments match values by *name*; a list passed in is shared with the caller, so changing it inside the function changes it outside, whereas reassigning the parameter does not. A module such as `math` is brought in with `import`, optionally under a shorter alias.

recap.nextHook: Functions and imports can both fail: a name may be missing, a file may be absent, a value may be unusable. The next lesson shows how to handle those failures without hiding them.

lessons.title: Handle failure without hiding it

lead.text: When a line cannot do what it was asked, Python raises an **exception**, which *stops* the program at that line and prints the name of the problem. The call `int('unknown')` raises a `ValueError`, because the text is not a whole number. If you expect that failure, you can catch it: the lines under `try` run normally, and if one of them raises a `ValueError`, Python jumps to the lines under **except ValueError** and carries on from there.

afterFigure.text: **Name the exception you expect**, here `ValueError`, because a bare `except` would also swallow mistakes you did not expect, such as a misspelt name, and would hide them from you.

cases.label: Text converts
Text fails

lead.text: There are two common ways to deal with an entry that will not convert. A **fallback** replaces it with a stand-in value such as 0 and keeps the entry in the calculation, while skipping leaves the entry out altogether. The two policies give different results from the same data: a column of `'10'`, `'n/a'` and `'20'` totals 30 either way, but its average is 10 when the stand-in 0 is counted among three entries and 15 when the bad entry is skipped and only two are averaged.

*Neither* policy is right in general. A stand-in of 0 says that the true value was zero, which may be false, and skipping says that the entry does not exist, which may also be false, so the choice should be made deliberately and should be visible to whoever reads the result.

The simplest way to make skipping visible is a second [[accumulator|A name that collects a running total as a loop goes round. Met in 'For loops'.]] that counts the rejected entries alongside the total. Inside the loop, the `try` block adds the converted value to `total`, and the `except` block adds 1 to `rejected` and moves on to the next entry.

afterFigure.text: With `'2'`, `'bad'` and `'5'` the middle entry raises, so `total` is still 7 but `rejected` is 1, and the pair `(7, 1)` tells the reader what a bare 7 would *hide*. A total is only as trustworthy as **the count of what was dropped**, because skipping one entry in three gives a different report from skipping one in three thousand.

cases.label: Nothing rejected
One rejected

lead.text: Follow the two accumulators through one entry at a time.

workedSteps.text: Both accumulators start at 0.
'3' converts, so it is added to the total.
`'x'` raises a `ValueError`, so the `except` branch counts it and the total is left alone.
'8' and '5' convert and are added to the total.
The result is reported with its count.

lead.text: Now two entries fail.

workedSteps.text: The loop is the same as before, applied to this list.
Each entry that converts is added to `total`, and each entry that raises is left out of it.
Each entry that raises a `ValueError` adds 1 to `rejected`.

lead.text: A file that is opened must also be closed, or the operating system keeps it reserved and some of what was written may never be saved. The statement `with open('data.csv') as f:` opens the file, gives it the name `f` for the lines beneath, and closes it when those lines end, **even if one of them raises an exception**. Anything that behaves in this way is called a **context manager**.

Reading is then a loop over the file's lines. Each line arrives with a newline at its end, and a blank line is empty once stripped, so `int(line)` on a blank line raises a `ValueError` like any other bad entry. Because an [[empty string|The string '' with no characters, whose length is 0. Met in 'Past the end'.]] is `False` the test `if line.strip():` keeps only the lines that have content, which skips blanks without counting them as errors. The `with` statement guarantees that the file is closed; it says *nothing* about whether the contents are valid.

A path such as `data.csv` names no folder, so Python looks for the file in the **working directory**, the folder the program was launched from. A path of this kind is called a **relative path**, because what it points to depends on *where you stand*, whereas an absolute path such as `/home/ana/data/data.csv` starts from the root of the disk and names one file wherever the program runs. The same script, launched from two folders that each hold a `data.csv`, reads two different files, and from a folder that holds none it stops with a `FileNotFoundError`.
Calling `os.getcwd()`, after `import os`, shows which folder a relative path is being resolved against, and it is the first thing to check.

lessons.orientation: Handle expected failures visibly, count what you skip, and open files safely.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Every real data file holds something the program did not expect: a price typed as n/a, an empty line at the end, a count entered with a decimal point. When Python meets such a value in `int('n/a')` it does not guess; it stops with an error.

Some of these failures are expected, such as a few bad entries in a long column, and a program should handle them openly, by skipping them and reporting how many it skipped, while others are mistakes that should stop the program at once.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to catch an expected error, report what was skipped, and say which file a path refers to.
intro.whyItMatters: A cleaning step that quietly drops or replaces entries changes the answer, and the reader must be told.

recap.keyIdea: Catch the exception you expect, count what you skip, and let a with block close the file.

blocks.text: An exception stops the program unless it is caught, and the safe habit is to **name the exception you expect**, handle it with a fallback or a skip, and keep a count of what was skipped. A `with` block closes a file whatever happens inside it, though it does not check the contents, and a relative path is resolved against the working directory, so the same script can read different files from different folders.

recap.nextHook: Plain Python is slow and clumsy for calculations on thousands of numbers. The next module introduces NumPy arrays, which hold numbers in a grid and calculate on all of them at once.

lessons.title: Give data a shape

lead.text: After `import numpy as np`, the call `np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])` builds an **array** with two rows and three columns. Its **shape** is the pair `(2, 3)`, in which the first number counts the rows and the second the columns, and each direction along which the numbers are laid out is called an **axis**. An array whose shape has two numbers has two axes, which is what its attribute `ndim` reports, and its size, the total number of elements, is the product of the shape: 2 * 3 = 6.

The call `np.zeros((2, 3))` gives a grid of zeros with that shape, and `np.arange(6)` gives the numbers 0 to 5 in a single row, whose shape is `(6,)`. The double brackets in `np.zeros((2, 3))` are intended: the inner pair builds the [[tuple|A fixed row of values in round brackets that cannot be changed. Met in 'Tuples'.]] `(2, 3)`, which is passed as the one argument.

With a Python list the star operator does something unexpected: `values * 2` repeats the list. An array is built so that arithmetic acts on its elements, and the same expression doubles *each* one, without a loop.

afterFigure.text: **The operator belongs to the type**: the same symbol means repeat for a list and multiply for an array, so check which type a name holds before reading its arithmetic. All the elements of an array also share one type, which is what lets NumPy calculate in a single pass, whereas a list may mix numbers, text and other lists.

cases.label: A list
cases.code:
values = [2, 4, 6]
result = values * 2

cases.label: An array
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.array([2, 4, 6])
result = values * 2

lead.text: The method **reshape** returns the same elements arranged in a new [[shape|The number of elements along each axis of an array, written as a tuple such as (2, 3). Met in 'Arrays and shape'.]]. The elements keep their order and fill the new rows from left to right, so `np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)` gives the rows `[0, 1, 2]` and `[3, 4, 5]`. Because *no* element is added or dropped, the product of the new shape must equal the size you started with: six elements can become 2 by 3, 3 by 2, 1 by 6 or 6 by 1, but never 4 by 2, and NumPy raises a `ValueError` when the counts disagree.
Follow the elements of `np.arange(10)` into a grid, and watch the shape, the size and the number of axes.

workedSteps.text: The call `np.arange(10)` gives the numbers 0 to 9, so the size is 10.
Two rows of five use all ten elements, because 2 * 5 is 10.
The shape of the new array is (2, 5).
The size is still 10, and there are two axes.

lead.text: In `reshape` the value `-1` means *work this one out*: with 12 elements, `reshape(3, -1)` fixes three rows and leaves NumPy to divide 12 by 3, which gives 4 columns, while `reshape(-1, 2)` fixes two columns and gives 6 rows. Only one dimension may be `-1`, and the other numbers must divide the size exactly.

afterFigure.text: The `-1` is shorthand for **the division you would otherwise do by hand**, and it is most useful when the number of elements is not known at the time the code is written.

cases.label: Three rows
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12)
result = a.reshape(3, -1)

cases.label: Two columns
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12)
result = a.reshape(-1, 2)

lead.text: An array stores all its elements with one **dtype**, a type of fixed width. The dtype `int16` stores each whole number in 2 bytes, `int32` in 4 and `int64` in 8, where a byte holds eight [[binary|Written with only the digits 0 and 1, as a computer stores numbers. Met in 'Combining conditions'.]] digits, and the attribute `itemsize` reports the width. The memory an array needs is the number of elements times that width, so a million values at 8 bytes each take eight million bytes, and at 2 bytes each only two million.

The saving has a *cost*, because a fixed width can hold only a fixed range of numbers. The dtype `int16` covers -32768 to 32767, so a larger value cannot be stored correctly, and the default for whole numbers on most machines is `int64`, which is wide enough for almost any count.

cases.label: Two bytes each
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([12, 30], dtype=np.int16)
bytes_per_item = a.itemsize

cases.label: Eight bytes each
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([12, 30], dtype=np.int64)
bytes_per_item = a.itemsize

lessons.orientation: Build NumPy arrays and track their shape, size and element width.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A table of 3 rows and 4 columns can be held in a Python list of lists, but every calculation on it then needs a loop over the rows and, inside that, a loop over the columns. A NumPy array holds the same grid as a single object, with a shape that records how many rows and columns it has, and it calculates on every number in one step.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read an array's shape, reshape it correctly, and work out the memory its values take.
intro.whyItMatters: A wrong shape raises an error or, worse, silently combines the wrong numbers.

recap.keyIdea: An array is a grid whose shape fixes its elements, and reshape can rearrange them only if the counts agree.

blocks.text: An array holds elements of one dtype in a grid whose [[shape|The number of elements along each axis of an array, written as a tuple such as (2, 3). Met in 'Arrays and shape'.]] lists the rows first, and its size is the product of that shape. Arithmetic acts on each element, `reshape` lays the same elements out again and needs the same total, with `-1` standing for **one dimension worked out for you**, and the memory used is the size times the *width* of the dtype.

recap.nextHook: Shape and size say what an array holds. The next lesson uses them to calculate across rows or down columns, and shows how arrays of different shapes can still be combined.

lessons.title: Calculate across the right axis

lead.text: Two arrays of the same shape combine element by element, so `np.array([1, 2, 3]) * np.array([4, 5, 6])` multiplies the first element with the first, the second with the second and the third with the third, giving 4, 10 and 18. The star always means *matching* positions here and never the product of two matrices. When one operand is a single number, NumPy treats it as if it were repeated to fit the array, so `np.array([1, 2, 3]) + 5` adds 5 to every element, and this stretching of a smaller value to the [[shape|The number of elements along each axis of an array, written as a tuple such as (2, 3). Met in 'Arrays and shape'.]] of a larger array is called **broadcasting**.
The result has the shape of the larger operand, and the arrays you started with are left unchanged.
A calculation that combines many numbers into fewer is called a **reduction**. The methods `sum`, `mean`, `min` and `max` are reductions, so `np.array([4, 6, 8]).sum()` is 18 and its mean is 6.0.

On a grid the same call could mean several different things, depending on which numbers are combined with which. With no argument, `sum` adds every element of the grid into a single number, but a table usually needs one total per column or one per row, and NumPy has to be *told* which.

The argument `axis` says which [[axis|A direction along which the numbers of an array are laid out. Met in 'Arrays and shape'.]] disappears. With `axis=0` the rows are combined, so the numbers in each column are added together and the result has one entry per column. With `axis=1` the columns are combined, so the numbers in each row are added and the result has one entry per row. The shape gives a check: a `(2, 3)` array reduced along axis 0 leaves the shape `(3,)`, and along axis 1 it leaves `(2,)`, because the axis you reduce is the one *removed* from the shape.

afterFigure.text: Along axis 0 the columns give 5, 7 and 9, and along axis 1 the rows give 6 and 15. **The axis named in the call is the one that is removed**, and remembering this is easier than remembering which number goes with rows and which with columns.

cases.label: axis=0
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
result = a.sum(axis=0)

cases.label: axis=1
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
result = a.sum(axis=1)

lead.text: Take a grid of two rows and three columns, and ask for the total of each row.

workedSteps.text: Row totals mean that the columns are combined inside each row, so the axis to remove is axis 1.
The first row holds 2, 5 and 1.
The second row holds 4, 0 and 3.
The two totals make up the result.

lead.text: Now the opposite direction: one total for each column.

workedSteps.text: Column totals remove axis 0, so the numbers in each column are added together.
The result has one value for each column, and its first value comes from the first column.
The second value of the result comes from the second column.

lead.text: Broadcasting also works between arrays of different shapes. The shapes are compared from the last axis backwards, and two lengths are compatible when they are equal or when one of them is 1. A row of two numbers added to a grid with two columns is therefore stretched down the rows, and it is added to *each* row in turn.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the row `[10, 20]` is added to each row of the grid, giving `[11, 22]` and `[13, 24]`, so that the 10 lands in the first column and the 20 in the second. In the second case a single number is stretched in both directions. A row broadcasts down the rows **when its length matches the number of columns**, and if it matched neither, NumPy would raise a `ValueError`, which is a useful protection against combining the wrong numbers.

cases.label: Add a row
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
result = a + np.array([10, 20])

cases.label: Add a single number
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
result = a + 10

lead.text: Slicing a list builds a new list, as the lists lesson showed, but slicing an array *copies* nothing. The result is a **view**, a new array object that looks at the same numbers, so writing through the view changes the original. This saves memory when the data is large, and it also means that `b = a[:2]` gives two names for overlapping data, which is the [[alias|Another name for the same data. Met in 'Two names, one list'.]] trap again.

afterFigure.text: Use **copy()** whenever a slice will be modified and the original must survive.

cases.label: A view
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 4, 6])
b = a[:2]
b[0] = 99

cases.label: A copy
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 4, 6])
b = a[:2].copy()
b[0] = 99

lessons.orientation: Calculate across the right axis, combine arrays of different shapes, and know when a slice shares data.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: In the last lesson `values * 2` doubled every element of an array. Two cases need more than that rule: a single row applied to every row of a grid, and a grid reduced to one total for each column, where an argument called `axis` decides the direction in which the numbers are combined.
Both come down to which numbers are matched with which. A wrong match here rarely raises an error and instead returns a sensible-looking array with the wrong numbers in it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict an array calculation, reduce along the axis you intend, and tell a view from a copy.
intro.whyItMatters: Totals per column and per row are the first summaries of any table, and the wrong axis gives plausible wrong numbers.

recap.keyIdea: Choose the axis you want removed, and remember that a slice of an array shares its data unless you copy it.

blocks.text: Arrays combine element by element, and a smaller operand is stretched across a larger one when the **lengths match from the last axis**. A reduction such as `sum` removes the axis you name, so `axis=0` leaves one total per column and `axis=1` one per row. A slice of an array is a *view* that shares its data with the original, and only `copy()` separates them.

recap.nextHook: Arrays are often built from ranges of numbers or random draws. The next lesson separates arange from linspace and makes random numbers repeatable.

lessons.title: Generate values with clear boundaries

lead.text: The function `np.arange` builds an array of evenly spaced numbers by stepping. With one argument, `np.arange(5)` gives 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, and with three, `np.arange(2, 12, 3)` starts at 2 and adds 3 each time, giving 2, 5, 8 and 11. It follows the rule of `range` and of slices: the start is included, the stop is *not*, and the sequence ends with the last value below the stop.

afterFigure.text: **The number of values depends on the step**, and it is the span divided by the step, rounded up. With a decimal step this count is harder to predict, because repeated addition is subject to the rounding described in the types lesson, and a function that fixes the number of points is safer.

cases.label: One argument
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.arange(5)

cases.label: Start, stop, step
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.arange(2, 12, 3)

lead.text: The function `np.linspace` asks a different question. Instead of a step it takes the number of points wanted, so `np.linspace(0, 12, 4)` gives four points from 0 to 12, and it works out the spacing *itself*. **Both ends are included** by default, which makes n points leave n − 1 gaps between them, and the spacing is therefore the span divided by n − 1: here 12 divided by 3, which is 4.

afterFigure.text: The second case adds `endpoint=False`, which leaves the end out, so the same four points are spread over the span with a gap of 3 and the last one stops short at 9. Use `linspace` when the end value matters and the count is known, as with the axis of a chart, and `arange` when the step matters.

cases.label: Both ends
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.linspace(0, 12, 4)

cases.label: End left out
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.linspace(0, 12, 4, endpoint=False)

lead.text: Work out where the six points of `np.linspace(0, 10, 6)` fall, by counting the gaps between them.

workedSteps.text: Six points include both ends, so the first is 0 and the last is 10.
Between six points there are five gaps, and the five gaps share the span of 10 equally.
Adding the spacing from 0 gives every point in turn.

lead.text: Now five points from 2 to 14.

workedSteps.text: The span from the first point to the last is 14 − 2.
Five points that include both ends are separated by gaps of equal size.
Starting at 2 and adding the spacing once for each gap reaches the last point.

lead.text: Random numbers come from a **generator**, an object that produces a long sequence of values that behave as if they had been chosen by chance. You create one with `np.random.default_rng()` and ask it for numbers: `rng.integers(1, 7, size=6)` returns six whole numbers, each chosen *independently* from the allowed values. Each call carries on from where the last one stopped, so two successive calls give different numbers.

As in a [[slice|A piece taken between a start and a stop; the stop is not included. Met in 'Slicing'.]] and in `arange`, the low bound of `rng.integers` is included and the high bound is excluded. The call `rng.integers(1, 5)` can therefore return 1, 2, 3 or 4 and *never* 5, and the number of possible outcomes is high minus low, here 4. If a value must be reachable, **the high bound has to be one more than it**, and an off-by-one slip here changes every later result without raising an error.

Random draws that change on every run make a result *impossible* to check, because you cannot tell whether a difference comes from the method or from the numbers. A generator started with a **seed**, a whole number passed to `default_rng`, avoids this: it produces the same sequence every time it is started from that seed.

afterFigure.text: **The seed fixes the whole sequence and not each draw**: continuing the same generator gives new numbers, whereas restarting it from the same seed gives the old ones. Record the seed in any analysis that depends on random numbers.

cases.label: Seed 21
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
draws = rng.integers(1, 7, size=6)

cases.label: Seed 22
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(22)
draws = rng.integers(1, 7, size=6)

cases.label: Two fresh generators
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.random.default_rng(9).integers(0, 10, 4)
b = np.random.default_rng(9).integers(0, 10, 4)
equal = np.array_equal(a, b)

cases.label: One generator, two draws
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
a = rng.integers(0, 10, 4)
b = rng.integers(0, 10, 4)
equal = np.array_equal(a, b)

lessons.orientation: Generate arrays of numbers with exact boundaries, and make random draws repeatable.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: `np.arange(0, 10, 2)` gives 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8, while `np.linspace(0, 10, 6)` gives 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Both describe evenly spaced numbers from 0 towards 10, but the first is told the size of each step and stops before the end, while the second is told how many points are wanted and includes both ends.

Generated values like these supply the x values of a chart, a grid of thresholds or a sample of random draws to test a method, and in every case the difficulty lies at the boundary, in whether the end value is included and which whole numbers a random draw can return.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the values arange and linspace produce, state the range of a random integer call, and repeat a draw with a seed.
intro.whyItMatters: A boundary that is one out gives a sample, a chart axis or a simulation that is wrong without any error message.

recap.keyIdea: arange excludes its stop, linspace includes both ends, integers excludes its high bound, and a seed repeats a draw.

blocks.text: The function `arange` steps from a start and **excludes its stop**, `linspace` takes a count of points and *includes* both ends, so n points leave n − 1 equal gaps, and `rng.integers` excludes its high bound. A generator started from a seed gives the same sequence on every run, which is what makes an analysis that uses random numbers checkable.

recap.nextHook: Generated and typed arrays are small. The next module moves to real tables read from files, starting with how to load one and look at it before trusting it.

lessons.title: Meet a real table

lead.text: A **CSV** file, short for comma-separated values, stores a table as plain text with one row on each line and a comma between the fields of a row. The first line normally holds the column names, so a file that begins with the line `shop,units,price` and continues with `Bay,2,5` and `Hill,1,8` describes a table with three columns and, so far, two rows.

Nothing in the file says which fields are numbers. To the file they are all just *characters*, and the decision that 2 is a number and Bay is a word is made later, by whatever reads it, which is why the reading step deserves care.

After `import pandas as pd`, the call `pd.read_csv('sales.csv')` reads the file and returns a **DataFrame**, a table whose columns have names and whose rows are numbered from 0. The header line becomes the column names and is not counted as a row, so a file with one header line and ten lines of data gives a DataFrame with ten rows.

Each column holds values of a single type, which pandas *guesses* from the text: a column whose fields all look like whole numbers becomes integers, one with decimals becomes floats, and anything else stays as text.

A DataFrame has a [[shape|The number of rows and columns of a table or array, written as a pair. Met in 'Arrays and shape'.]] just as an array does: `df.shape` is the pair (rows, columns), so the table in the figure, with four rows and three columns, has the shape `(4, 3)`. Selecting a column by name, `df['units']`, returns a **Series**, a single labelled column of values, whereas putting the name inside a list, `df[['units']]`, returns a DataFrame with one column, which *keeps* the table form.

afterFigure.text: A single name **gives a Series** and a list of names **gives a table**, so the number of brackets decides which of the two you receive.

cases.label: One name
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df['units']
shape = df.shape

cases.label: A list of names
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df[['units']]
shape = result.shape

lead.text: Both selections name the same column of the table on the previous screen, but they return different kinds of object.

workedSteps.text: A single name inside one pair of brackets picks out one column.
The result is a Series of four values, with no columns of its own.
A list of names inside a second pair of brackets picks out a table.
The result is a DataFrame with the same four rows and one column.

lead.text: The method **head** returns the first five rows when called as `df.head()`, and the first three as `df.head(3)`. It returns a new, smaller DataFrame as a preview and leaves `df` itself with *all* its rows, and `df.tail()` does the same for the last rows, where problems such as a stray totals line often sit.
Together with `df.shape` and `df.dtypes`, which lists the type of every column, `head` is the standard first look at a table you did not build yourself.

When pandas guesses a column's type it sees only the characters, and a field such as 0012 looks like a whole number, so it is read as the integer 12 and the leading zeros disappear. For an identifier it destroys information, because 0012 and 12 may name different things and the code may need its original length. A value you would *never* add or average, such as a postcode, a phone number or a product code, **should be read as text**.

You say so when reading the file: `pd.read_csv('sales.csv', dtype={'code': str})` reads the column called `code` as text and keeps every character. The [[dtype|The type in which every element of an array or column is stored. Met in 'Bytes per element'.]] argument names the type for each column you want to fix.

The function `read_csv` expects commas. A file whose fields are separated by semicolons, as is common in exports from systems that use the comma as a decimal mark, contains no commas to split on, so each line is read as one long field and the table has a single column. You give the real **separator** with the argument `sep`, as in `pd.read_csv('file.csv', sep=';')`, which splits every line at the semicolons.
The mistake raises *no* error, which makes the shape the quickest check: a table that should have four columns and has one was read with the wrong separator.

lessons.orientation: Read a CSV file into a DataFrame and check it before trusting it.
